title: Ashtpadi 2, salok: destroyer of pain
hookLine: deen darad dukh bhanjanaa: He destroys the pain of the humble (Sukhmani 2)

lines: PAIN THAT DOESN'T MAKE THE NEWS.
cards: There's a kind of pain that doesn't make the news. The person who lost their job and hasn't told anyone yet. The old man whose children call twice a year.
The new immigrant who can't read the letters arriving in the mail. Nobody stands up for them. They don't have someone to ring, a cousin who knows someone, a name that opens doors.
In Guru Arjan's Punjab there were words for people like that, and the second ashtpadi of Sukhmani opens by naming them, and who stands with them.

teach.h: DEEN, DARAD, DUKH: THE HUMBLE'S PAIN.
teach.b: Here is the salok: deen darad dukh bhanjanaa, ghat ghat naath anaath. Word by word. Deen: the poor, the humble, the ones with nothing to bargain with.
Darad: pain, the ache that won't go away. Dukh: suffering, the opposite of the sukh in Sukhmani.

teach.h: BHANJANAA: THE ONE WHO BREAKS IT.
teach.b: Bhanjanaa: the breaker, the one who smashes it to pieces. So: the One who breaks the pain and suffering of the humble. Then ghat ghat naath: master of every heart, every single body.
Then anaath, and here readers differ. Some translators take it as another name for God: the One with no master above.
Others read naath anaath together: master of the masterless. In everyday Punjabi an anaath is an orphan, someone with no one, and on that reading the One protects those with no protector.
The second line is Nanak's own voice.

teach.h: NANAK COMES TO THE SHELTER TOO.
teach.b: In paraphrase: I have come to Your shelter; God, be with Nanak. Notice two things. The salok doesn't say pain never comes.

It says there's a breaker of pain, and names who the breaker stands with: not the powerful, but the humble, and on one reading the unprotected. And look where the Guru puts himself: not above the deen, but among them.
He comes to the shelter too. In the days ahead, this ashtpadi walks into the hardest places a person goes, where no family can follow.
But it begins here, with a name for God anyone in pain can call on: the one who breaks it.

how: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite this salok at the start of the second ashtpadi, and some say it, or the whole bani, for someone who is ill or suffering.

o: a debt that must be paid back in full
suffering, sorrow: the opposite of sukh
the anger felt at someone's wrongdoing

games.q: the second salok, word by word — tap the pairs.

s: the salok says pain never comes to the humble
it says there is a breaker of pain who stands with them.
in Punjabi, anaath can mean an orphan
some read the salok as master of the masterless; others take anaath as God, the One with no master.
in the salok, Nanak comes to God's shelter too
I have come to Your shelter; God, be with Nanak.

games.q: the second ashtpadi opens with a name for God. who does the salok say God stands with?
o: the humble and those in pain.
games.why: deen darad dukh bhanjanaa, ghat ghat naath: the breaker of the humble's pain, master of every heart.

practice: Let one person come to mind whose pain you know about, or who you sense has no one to ring, and see them as clearly as you can.
If you pray, say the salok's first words for them, deen darad dukh bhanjanaa, or simply Waheguru; if not, hold them in mind and wish them one thing: that the pain breaks, a little.

wordCard.voice: Dukh, suffering: Sukhmani's second section, whose salok names God the breaker of the pain of the humble and the master of every heart.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: dukh, suffering; the opposite of the sukh in Sukhmani.

carryVoice: Your line: he breaks pain. And the Guru stands among the humble, not above them. Until tomorrow.
